items.stem: Which property describes how well a material lets electric current flow through it?

options.text: Flexibility
Hardness
Electrical conductivity
Melting point

items.explanation: Electrical conductivity measures how easily electricity flows through a material. Metals conduct well; plastic, wood, and ceramic block current.

items.stem: An engineer needs the body of a frying pan to spread heat quickly and evenly. Which property matters most, and which material fits best?

options.text: Thermal conductivity, so choose metal
Flexibility, so choose plastic
Melting point, so choose wood
Hardness, so choose ceramic

items.explanation: The pan's job is to move heat into the food, so thermal conductivity matters most. Metals are excellent heat conductors, which is why pans are metal.

items.stem: The same frying pan needs a handle that stays cool to hold. Why is the handle often made of wood or plastic instead of metal?

options.text: Wood and plastic are stronger than metal
Wood and plastic are poor thermal conductors, so heat does not reach your hand
Wood and plastic have higher melting points than metal
Metal costs too much to use for a handle

items.explanation: A cool handle needs low thermal conductivity. Wood and plastic barely carry heat, so it stays in the pan instead of traveling to your hand.

items.stem: Ductility is the property that lets a material be...

options.text: scratched by a harder material
heated until it glows
dissolved in water
stretched and bent into a new shape without breaking

items.explanation: Ductility is how much a material can be stretched or bent into a new shape without breaking. Metals are ductile, which is why cans and car bodies are stamped from them.

items.stem: Plastic is wrapped around the metal core of an electrical wire. What does this best show about choosing materials?

options.text: Plastic conducts electricity better than metal
The wire would work just as well made entirely of plastic
Each part is chosen for a different job: metal carries the current, plastic blocks it to keep you safe
Plastic is the strongest material available

items.explanation: The metal core and plastic coating each do a different job. Metal is chosen because it conducts, plastic because it blocks current and protects the user. Different properties, different jobs.

items.stem: A material must line the inside of a 900-degree oven without melting or softening. Which choice fits best?

options.text: Plastic, because it is light
A ceramic, because it has a very high melting point
Wood, because it is easy to shape
Rubber, because it is flexible

items.explanation: Surviving extreme heat depends on melting point. Ceramics have very high melting points and stay solid, which is why ovens and kilns are lined with ceramic.

items.stem: Diego says steel is "the best material" because it is strong. What is the problem with his thinking?

options.text: There is no single best material; the best choice depends on what the part must do
Steel is actually the weakest material
Aluminum is always better than steel
Strength never matters in a design

items.explanation: No material is best at everything. The best choice always depends on the job. Steel is great for a chain but too heavy for a whole bike frame.

items.stem: A bike tire must grip the road and bend on every turn without cracking. Which property matters most, and which material is used?

options.text: Hardness, and ceramic
Melting point, and metal
Electrical conductivity, and copper
Flexibility, and rubber, which is a plastic

items.explanation: A tire flexes constantly, so flexibility matters most. Rubber, a type of plastic, bends over and over without cracking, which is why tires are rubber.

items.stem: Why are floor tiles usually made from ceramic instead of wood?

options.text: Ceramic is cheaper than every other material
Ceramic is flexible, so it bounces back
Ceramic is hard and resists scratches and wear from foot traffic
Ceramic conducts electricity safely

items.explanation: A busy floor gets scraped all day, so hardness matters most. Ceramic is very hard and resists scratches and dents, while wood is softer and wears down.

items.stem: An engineer picks aluminum for a bike frame and rubber for the tires. What best describes how she is thinking?

options.text: She picks the strongest material for every part
She matches each part's material to the job that part has to do
She picks the cheapest material for every part
She uses whatever material is easiest to find

items.explanation: This is the core engineering move: match the material to the job. A light aluminum frame and grippy rubber tires each fit what that part needs to do.
